graph_effect.label: Xu et al. 2020 Chicago homicide, per 5 C mean temperature lag 0-7 (graph stores 0.095 as an odds ratio)

graph_evidence.summary: Lyons et al. 2022, 100 US cities 2015-2020, RR 1.17 (1.12 to 1.21) for the 84th percentile of daily maximum temperature against the city median; matches the abstract (PMID 36525273, read 12 Nov 2026). The only gun-violence temperature finding in the graph; it covers Chicago and New York but reports no city-specific estimate.

Xu et al. 2020 (PMID 32738768) gives intentional homicide +9.5% (4.3 to 15.0) per 5 C in Chicago and +8.8% (1.5 to 16.6) in New York, lag 0-7; the graph stores these as odds ratios 0.095 and 0.088 (the abstract gives percent increases, so the stored values are mis-scaled). Rahman et al. 2023, California, +4.9% (PMID 36858215). This is the graph's one direct two-city comparison, and it shows Chicago and New York within 1 point of each other.

notes:
Same negative binomial model as heat-shootings, fitted to 6,085 days and 41,063 cases in Chicago from 2010 (when the portal's non-fatal shooting series begins) to 31 August 2026. Midway TMAX was missing on 0.03% of days. Within-city seasonality is absorbed by month and year terms, so the estimate describes day-to-day deviations from the month's level.

After the referee (13 Nov 2026): the referee rebuilt the daily series, obtained the same estimate (1.131, 1.120 to 1.143) and found it inside the transfer band under six further specifications; errors that allow for serial correlation widen the interval by about a tenth (1.119 to 1.144). What transfers is the average slope and not the shape of the dose-response. Fitted separately below and above 20 C, Chicago's slope is 1.148 (1.133 to 1.164) below and 1.104 (1.084 to 1.124) above, and New York's from 2010 is 1.137 (1.112 to 1.164) below and 1.174 (1.139 to 1.210) above. Chicago flattens on hot days and New York steepens, and the average slopes agree in part because Chicago has more cold days. The claim transfer-chicago-hot-end addresses the shape. New York refitted from 2010 gives 1.151 (1.132 to 1.170), so the difference in periods does not matter.
